name: Pedro Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Pedro. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say out loud and, separately, what you really think. To begin, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's split, which is why I like it. I work for a timber-frame company that builds wall and floor panels in a shed out by the old rail yard, then we put them up on site. Three days a week I'm in the factory checking panels off the line, two days I'm on site craning them into place and fixing them. A three-bed house goes up weathertight in four days, which still blows my mind.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much do you use technology in that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: All day. I run the cut lists through an app, I ask a chatbot about fixing details and building rules when the drawings are vague, and I've got a little AI voice note thing that writes my site diary. My boss jokes that I'm the factory's unofficial IT guy. The older carpenters call me the professor, which is generous, because I left the tech college with a trade certificate like everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. Bit disappointing, to be honest. I'd have liked more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent set of tools and people oversold it. I'd probably post something like, AI didn't take my job, it just writes my site diary. And I'd keep showing the lads the tricks I use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's fine either way. I've got a good wage, around eight months in savings and a bit in an index fund, and I share a flat with my mate Kofi, so rent's low. A plateau just means I keep doing what I enjoy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, keep learning the tools as they get a bit better. I'd probably push my boss to let me trial the panel scanner the supplier's been showing us. And I'd keep putting a few hundred a month into the fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe, like a film that ends early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you have hoped for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Machines doing the lifting and the dull bits, so carpenters keep their backs past fifty. My dad was a bricklayer and couldn't lift his grandkids by sixty. That's what I wanted tech to fix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any downside for you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that the bosses keep the small savings and nobody else sees them. That's how it usually goes. The time saved never shows up in anyone's payslip.

S0.say: I'd say AI is a decent set of tools that people oversold, and I'd post that it didn't take my job, it just writes my site diary. I'd keep showing the other carpenters the tricks I use.
S0.think: It's fine either way for him: good wage, about eight months of savings, an index fund and low rent sharing with a friend. A plateau just means he keeps doing work he enjoys.
S0.do: Keeps learning the tools as they improve and pushes his boss to trial a panel scanner. Keeps putting a few hundred a month into his index fund.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit flat, like a film that ends early.
S0.quote: My dad was a bricklayer and couldn't lift his grandkids by sixty.
S0.fieldNote: Pedro sounds let down by a plateau because he wanted technology to save workers' bodies. His father's injuries shape his hopes. He already notes that bosses keep the savings, which hints at his politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one's basically my job already, just faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good if it's managed well. Factory-built homes are faster and safer, but the gains have to go to the workers too, through better pay and shorter weeks. I'd say unions should push for a four-day week, not fight the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I come out ahead. I know the factory side and the site side, and that's exactly the mix that gets hired when things change. The guys I worry about are the ones who only know traditional framing and won't touch a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the robotics operator course the local college started, the one for automated nailing lines, and do it at night. I'd put some savings into it if the company didn't pay. And I'd talk to the union about setting up training on the factory floor for everyone, not just me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Honestly, a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd come out ahead. Does that sit easily with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not totally. It feels a bit like being the one who finds a lifeboat. That's why I'd push the training for everyone, because otherwise I'm just the guy who got lucky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who specifically would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek, who's been framing for thirty years and does it beautifully by eye. He told me once he's never sent a text message. He'd be lost, and he's the one who taught me.

S1.say: I'd say factory-built homes are faster and safer, but the gains have to reach workers through better pay and shorter weeks. Unions should push for a four-day week, not fight machines.
S1.think: He thinks he'd come out ahead because he knows both factory and site work. He worries about carpenters who only know traditional framing and won't use screens.
S1.do: Signs up for a night course in operating automated nailing lines, paying from savings if the company won't. Asks the union to set up training on the factory floor for everyone.
S1.quote: It feels a bit like being the one who finds a lifeboat.
S1.fieldNote: Pedro is clearly a winner in this picture and he knows it, which makes him slightly uncomfortable. His progressive outlook shows in wanting gains shared and training for all. Marek, his mentor, is the person he worries about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Wow. Two years. That's the whole factory and both sides of my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that we need a basic income and some public share in these companies, straight away. If machines do everything, the profits have to be shared or society breaks. I'd be online a lot, probably too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my skills only buy me a few months more than everyone else. I'd probably get to babysit the robots for a while, but that's a job for one person per shed, not twenty. My savings would last, but my plans wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd ask to move onto the automation side, whatever it is, before the queue forms. I'd keep saving harder, stop the fund contributions and keep cash. And I'd get together with people from work to look at a co-op, where workers own a share of the machines, because owning the robots is the only safe spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Busy-anxious, though. I'd be the one making spreadsheets at midnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years take away that the slower ones give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being ahead. With two years, being early doesn't matter much, because everybody gets hit within months of each other. With five or ten, the early people really do get a head start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Kofi?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we should stop talking about moving to a bigger place. He's a delivery driver, so he'd be hit even sooner than me. We'd probably sit on the balcony and plan a business we can't afford.

S2.say: I'd say we need a basic income and a public share in these companies straight away, because if machines do everything the profits have to be shared. I'd be online a lot, probably too much.
S2.think: His skills only buy him a few months more than everyone else, maybe looking after the robots, but that's a job for one person per shed, not twenty. His savings would last but his plans wouldn't.
S2.do: Asks to move onto the automation side before the queue forms, stops index fund payments and keeps cash. Gets colleagues together to explore a worker co-op that owns a share of the machines.
S2.quote: I'd probably get to babysit the robots for a while, but that's a job for one person per shed, not twenty.
S2.fieldNote: Even Pedro's adaptability can't outrun a two-year deadline, and he says the speed cancels out being early. He turns anxiety into activity, from co-op plans to politics. Owning the machines, not working beside them, is where he thinks safety lies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Better. That's enough time to actually build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan properly, so let's get worker ownership and a basic income designed now, not in a panic. I'd join a campaign group and actually go to the meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is enough to get myself into a good spot, maybe running an automated line or helping start a co-op. But the end point still worries me, because when it arrives, even that job could go. I'd be thirty-two and very good at a job robots also do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd finish the robotics course and move into the automation team. I'd start a small side business with Kofi programming and fitting smart home kits, to have a second income. And I'd push politically for the co-op model every chance I got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Hopeful, with a knot in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The side business, isn't that also something AGI would do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, fair. You're right. I guess the point is learning to run something, not the thing itself, so when the end comes I'm an owner, not just staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the next five years feel at work, day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably exciting, then sad. Each year a few more of the older guys would leave. I'd hate being the one showing the machine how Marek does his joints.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to plan properly, so worker ownership and a basic income should be designed now, not in a panic. I'd join a campaign group and actually go to meetings.
S3.think: Five years is enough to get himself into a good position running an automated line or helping start a co-op. But when the end point arrives even that job could go, leaving him 32 and skilled at something robots also do.
S3.do: Finishes the robotics course in the first year and joins the automation team. Starts a side business with his flatmate fitting smart home kits, and pushes for the co-op model politically.
S3.feel: Uneasy: hopeful, with a knot in it.
S3.quote: I'd hate being the one showing the machine how Marek does his joints.
S3.fieldNote: When I pointed out that AGI could do the side business too, he took it calmly and reframed it as learning to own. The guilt about training machines on his mentor's skills came up unprompted. Five years gives him room to build rather than scramble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Now we're talking. That's basically a career plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to make this good for everyone, if we start now: a four-day week, worker-owned factories, and income for people as jobs go. I'd say it at work and online, and I'd mean it as a plan, not a slogan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years makes me fairly relaxed about myself. I'd be thirty-seven, I'd have savings, skills on both sides and, if things go right, a share in a co-op. My real question would be whether we use the decade or waste it like we did with climate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the robotics course, then an engineering diploma part time over three or four years. I'd invest steadily, maybe buy into the co-op or put more into the fund. And I'd help set up training with the union, so the Mareks of the world have a way through too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Ten years is a long time to get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say calm, but you also said the end point worries you. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I guess. For me personally, calm. For everyone else, it depends on whether we get organised, and history isn't great on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger self, leaving college?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the machines but stay friends with the old guys. The old guys know why things are built the way they are. The machines just know how.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to make this good for everyone if we start now, with a four-day week, worker-owned factories and income as jobs go. I'd say it as a plan, not a slogan.
S4.think: Ten years makes him fairly relaxed about himself: at 37 he'd have savings, skills on both sides and hopefully a co-op share. His real question is whether society uses the decade or wastes it like climate.
S4.do: Takes the robotics course, then a part-time engineering diploma over three or four years. Invests steadily in a co-op or his fund, and helps the union set up training for older carpenters.
S4.feel: Mostly calm; ten years feels like plenty of time to get ready.
S4.quote: The old guys know why things are built the way they are. The machines just know how.
S4.fieldNote: Pedro separates his own fate from society's quite clearly, calm for himself and doubtful about collective action. He accepted the contradiction easily when named. He thinks in plans and timelines more than in feelings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because nobody gets a head start and nobody has a plan. What would help is a basic income starting quickly and laws that let workers own a share of the machines that replace them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what we'd do with the time. If robots build the houses, I'd still want to build a boat or a table, just for me. Work was never only about the money, it's about making something you can stand next to.

headlineQuote: Work was never only about the money, it's about making something you can stand next to.
portrait: Pedro Reyes is a 27-year-old carpenter splitting his week between a timber-frame factory and building sites, sharing a flat with a friend and holding eight months of savings plus an index fund. He uses AI every day and is seen as the factory's unofficial tech person. He's calm in the mild pictures and sees himself coming out ahead, but uneasy about older colleagues like his mentor Marek. Only the two-year AGI picture makes him anxious, and he answers it with co-op plans, politics and spreadsheets.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because nobody would get a head start and nobody would have a plan.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income that starts quickly and laws that let workers own a share of the machines that replace them.
